title: Solomon Asks for Wisdom
summary: Solomon marries Pharaoh's daughter and worships at the high places, especially the great one at Gibeon, where the LORD appears to him in a dream and invites him to ask for anything. Solomon asks for an understanding heart to judge God's people, and God, pleased, promises him unmatched wisdom along with riches and honor, and long life if he obeys. Back in Jerusalem, two prostitutes bring Solomon a dispute over a living baby, and his command to divide the child reveals the true mother, so that all Israel sees God's wisdom in him.
story: The throne is secure after chapter 2; now the question is what kind of king Solomon will be. This chapter gives the best answer the book will offer. Solomon's request at Gibeon is humble and other-centered: he calls himself a little child and asks not for power or revenge but for the ability to judge God's people well. God answers generously. The famous case of the two mothers follows immediately, as proof that the gift is real. Yet the chapter opens with two notes that will matter later: a marriage alliance with Egypt and worship at the high places. Both are presented mildly here, but the reader who knows Deuteronomy hears a warning. Chapter 11 will show where foreign marriages and divided worship led.
historical:
Solomon's reign is usually dated from about 970 to 930 BC. A marriage to a daughter of Pharaoh is a remarkable claim, because Egyptian kings of earlier periods were known for refusing to send their daughters abroad as wives for foreign rulers. By Solomon's time, however, Egypt was weaker and divided, ruled by the Twenty-first Dynasty from Tanis in the Nile delta, and such alliances became more likely. The Bible does not name this Pharaoh; some scholars suggest Siamun, but that identification is a proposal, not a certainty. According to 1 Kings 9:16, Pharaoh captured the city of Gezer and gave it to his daughter as a dowry.

Gibeon lay about six miles northwest of Jerusalem. First Chronicles 16:39 and 2 Chronicles 1:3 say the tabernacle, the portable tent-sanctuary from Moses' day, and its bronze altar stood there at this time, which would explain why it was called the great high place. The ark itself was in Jerusalem, in the tent David had pitched for it (verse 15).
cultural:
High places were local hilltop or raised worship sites with altars, common throughout Canaan. Before the temple was built, Israelites used them to worship the LORD, and the narrator here explains rather than condemns: there was not yet a house for the Name of the LORD. Deuteronomy 12, however, had looked forward to one place of worship that God would choose, and later in Kings the high places become a mark of failure. The word except in verse 3 signals a reservation.

Dreams were a recognized way for gods to communicate with kings in the ancient Near East, and royal inscriptions from Egypt and Mesopotamia describe kings receiving divine messages in dreams, often at the start of a reign. The request for wisdom to judge also reflects the king's main duty in that world: kings were the highest court of appeal, and ancient law collections such as Hammurabi's present the king as the one who establishes justice. That two prostitutes could bring their case directly to the king shows that justice was meant to reach the lowest in society. The case had no witnesses, so the king had to find the truth another way.
literary: The chapter has three parts: a short introduction (verses 1-3), the dream at Gibeon (verses 4-15), and the judgment of the two mothers (verses 16-28). The dream is structured as a conversation: God's open offer, Solomon's reply (recalling God's love to David, confessing his inexperience, and making his request), and God's answer, which grants what was asked, adds what wasn't, and attaches a condition. The trial scene uses repetition skillfully. The women's claims are mirror images, and Solomon repeats them back (verse 23) to show the deadlock before cutting through it. The narrator never says in advance what Solomon intends; the reader, like the court, learns the point only when the true mother cries out. The last verse ties the two halves together: all Israel saw that the wisdom of God was in him.

outline.t: Pharaoh's daughter and the high places
The dream at Gibeon and Solomon's request
God grants wisdom, riches, and honor
Two mothers and one living child
The king's judgment reveals the true mother

doctrines.note: Wisdom is presented as a gift from God, received by asking. Its purpose is not private cleverness but the ability to govern justly and to discern between good and evil for the sake of others.

Solomon's request is a model of prayer: it begins by remembering God's faithfulness, admits need honestly, and asks for what serves God's people. God delights in the request and gives more than was asked.
The king's first duty is justice, especially for those with no one else to defend them. The chapter shows the ideal of Israelite kingship: a ruler whose power serves right judgment.

words.note: Shama, to hear or listen. Solomon asks literally for a hearing heart (verse 9), translated understanding heart. In Hebrew the heart is the seat of thought and will, and a hearing heart is one that listens to God and to the people it judges. The word Shema, Israel's great confession (Deuteronomy 6:4), comes from the same verb.

Bin, to understand or discern, to tell things apart. It appears four times, in Solomon's request and God's answer. It describes the ability to see beneath appearances, which is exactly what the case of the two mothers requires.

Bamah, high place, a raised site of worship. Here it is described without harsh judgment, since the temple did not yet exist, but the word will become a refrain of criticism throughout Kings as later kings fail to remove the high places.

Rachamim, compassion or tender love, related to the word for womb. The true mother's compassion for her son reveals her identity. The same word is used of God's own compassion toward his people, a mother's love as a picture of God's.

christ: Solomon's wisdom is a gift that points beyond him. Jesus himself drew the comparison: the Queen of the South came to hear Solomon's wisdom, and something greater than Solomon is here (Matthew 12:42). Paul calls Christ the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24) and says that in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). Where Solomon asked for a hearing heart to judge justly, Isaiah's promised son of David would have the Spirit of wisdom and understanding and would judge the poor with righteousness, not by what his eyes see or his ears hear (Isaiah 11:2-4). The New Testament also takes up the pattern of asking God for wisdom and receiving it generously (James 1:5). These are connections drawn from the wider story, not predictions within the chapter.

hard.q: Was Solomon really wiser than anyone before or after, and does the chapter approve of his worship at the high places?
hard.a: God's promise that there would never be another like Solomon (verse 12) uses the language of royal praise common in the ancient Near East, where kings were described as incomparable; it expresses the greatness of the gift rather than making a precise historical ranking, though many readers take it at face value as well. On the high places, the narrator explains the practice (no temple yet existed) but also qualifies Solomon's devotion with the word except. Most interpreters see a gentle warning: Solomon's heart for God is real, but it is not undivided, and that seed of compromise grows later. Some see nothing negative here at all, noting that God meets Solomon at a high place. Both readings agree that the chapter's main point is the gift of wisdom and its right use.

questions: If God said to you, Ask, and I will give it to you, what would you ask for, and what does that reveal about your heart?
Solomon asked for a hearing heart. Whom do you need to listen to more carefully before making judgments?
The true mother was willing to give up her claim to save her child's life. What does love willing to lose look like in your relationships?
